title: The Oath of Office

narrative.text: Republic Square is full. Twenty thousand people, maybe more. The crowd stretches past the fountain, past the ministry steps, into the side streets. They have been waiting since dawn.
You stand behind the curtain at the top of the steps. Through the gap in the fabric you can see the podium. The microphone. The book of oaths. The chair where Halvek sat for twenty-three years.
Two minutes, Chancellor. The Chief Justice is ready.
Your speech. Three versions on the podium. National unity — safe, expected, no enemies made. Reform mandate — bolder, names the problems, some in the old guard will take it personally. The third...
The third is the one you wrote yourself at 2am. I read it. It's good. It will also terrify half the Assembly.

monologue: Twenty thousand people. Every word I say in the next ten minutes will be printed, quoted, misquoted, and remembered. Vyktor prepared the safe version. The bold version. And then there's mine — the one I wrote when I couldn't sleep, when I was thinking about my father and what he would have wanted to hear from this podium. The question is not which speech is best. The question is which chancellor I want to be when I walk back through that curtain.

choices.text: The national unity speech. Bring the country together first. Fight later.
The reform mandate. Name the problems. Let them know what's coming.
My speech. The one I wrote at 2am.

narrative.text: You step through the curtain. The sound hits you like a wall — twenty thousand people, and then, as you reach the podium, silence. Complete silence. The kind that only happens when a crowd is holding its breath.
You look down at the speech. Then you look up at the faces. You begin.

Citizens of the Republic. I stand here not as a victor, but as a servant. The election is over. The campaign is over. What begins today is harder than either of those things — the work of governing a country that has been through too much, and still believes it can be something better.
A murmur through the crowd. Not applause — something quieter. Recognition.

I know there are people in this square today who did not vote for me. I know there are people watching from home who are afraid of what this government might do. I am asking for your patience. Not your agreement — your patience. Judge us by what we actually do. Hold us to it. That is your right and I am asking you to use it.
To your left, Jonas is very still. He has heard you give a hundred speeches. His expression says this one is different.

The Republic does not belong to any party. It does not belong to any faction, any family, any interest. It belongs to the person in Kravenstal who went to work at five this morning. It belongs to the student in Dravenhollow who is the first in her family to finish secondary school. It belongs to the old man in Thornfeld who remembers what this country was before it forgot itself. It belongs to all of you. I will not forget that. Thank you.
The applause begins slowly — then swells. Not the manufactured roar of a rally. Something more genuine. Twenty thousand people deciding, individually, that this might be real.

choices.text: Take a moment. Look at the crowd. Remember this.
Look at Jonas. He's the reason any of this matters.

narrative.text: You step to the podium. The crowd falls quiet. You set aside the safe version of the speech without looking at it.
Citizens of the Republic. I am going to speak plainly today, because I think plain speaking is exactly what has been missing from this podium for twenty-three years.
Somewhere in the crowd, someone cheers. A single voice. Then others join.

This government inherited a deficit of money and a deficit of trust. I will not pretend otherwise. The books have been managed dishonestly. Institutions that were meant to protect you were used against you. People in positions of public trust treated those positions as private property. That ends today. Not as a promise — as a fact.
In the front row, three Assembly members are not applauding. You notice them. You continue.

Reform is not punishment. I want to be clear about that. We are not here to settle scores. We are here to build something that works — for everyone, including the people who are nervous about what comes next. A government that operates honestly does not threaten honest people. Remember that.
Vyktor, at the side of the stage, makes a small note. You have named the problem without naming names. It is a careful line to walk and you have walked it.

The next four years will be difficult. I am not going to stand here and tell you they will not be. Change is difficult. Accountability is difficult. But the alternative — another decade of managed decline, of quiet corruption, of a country that stopped believing in itself — that is harder. We choose the difficult thing. Thank you.
The applause is loud and immediate. Half the square. Then more. The three Assembly members in the front row eventually join in — slowly, reluctantly, but they join.

choices.text: Glance up at the silent balconies. Let them know you saw.
Stay focused on the crowd. This speech was for them.

narrative.text: You step to the podium. You do not look at any of the prepared speeches. You look at the crowd for a long moment — long enough that Vyktor, at the side of the stage, shifts his weight.
Then you begin. The words from 2am. The ones you were not sure you would actually say.
I almost gave you a different speech today. A safer one. My chief of staff prepared three versions. They were all good. They would all have served the moment. I am not going to give you any of them.
A ripple through the crowd. Curiosity. Attention sharpening.

My father worked in the Kravenstal foundries for thirty-one years. He never once appeared on a list, attended a party meeting, or asked anything from the people who ran this country. He just worked. When he got sick, the state hospital had a six-month waiting list. He waited. He died on that list. That is not a political story. That is just what happened to an ordinary man in a country that forgot ordinary men existed.
Complete silence. Twenty thousand people and no sound at all.

I am not here because I wanted power. I am here because I got tired of watching what happened to my father happen to other people's fathers. I am here because someone had to be. And if I fail — if this government fails — I want you to remember that I stood here today and told you exactly why I came. Hold me to it. Please.

The silence holds for three full seconds after you finish. Then it breaks — not into applause exactly, but into something louder and less organized. People shouting. People crying. Someone near the front is just saying yes, yes, yes.
Jonas has turned away. You know why. You give him a moment.
That was not one of the three speeches.
It was better than all of them.

choices.text: Let yourself feel it. Just for a moment.
Stay composed. The work starts now.

narrative.text: Behind the curtain. The noise of the crowd still audible. Your hands are steady. You didn't expect them to be steady.
Well. That's done. The Assembly will have opinions. The press will have opinions. Everyone will have opinions.
What matters now is tomorrow morning. First cabinet meeting. Nine people in a room and every one of them already has an agenda.

choices.text: How did I do?
I don't need a review. What's first on the desk?
Where's Jonas? I want to see him before anything else.

narrative.text: Jonas is waiting at the bottom of the steps. Tomas is holding his hand. Liora is pretending she wasn't crying.
You looked like a chancellor up there.
He says it simply. The way he says everything. No performance. No qualification.
You sounded like you.
That is the best thing anyone has said to you today.

choices.text: Hold his hand. Just for a second, before the cameras find us.
Thank him with a look. Then turn back to Vyktor.

narrative.text: You looked up at the balconies. They saw you look. Good. Let them know the new chancellor counts the silence as carefully as the applause.
You made some enemies today.
Cabinet meeting tomorrow morning. We should talk about who sits where.

choices.text: Let's talk tonight. I want the names in front of me before I sleep.
Tomorrow. Tonight I'm having dinner with my family.

narrative.text: For three seconds — no more — you close your eyes. You hear the crowd. You feel the wood of the podium under your hands. You think of your father. He would have been in the crowd, not on the stage. He never wanted the stage.
But he would have wanted this.
You open your eyes. The work begins.

choices.text: Compose yourself. Walk back through the curtain.

narrative.text: You want honesty or encouragement?

The speech was good. The delivery was better. Three people on that balcony are already calling their lawyers and two of them are calling Vael. You have about six weeks before the goodwill runs out and the real opposition starts.
Use them.

choices.text: Six weeks. That's more than I expected.
It's not enough.

narrative.text: You find Jonas in the corridor behind the stage. He's looking at a painting on the wall — one of the old chancellors, someone whose name neither of you remember.
I counted. You paused three times during the speech. The third one was the longest.
I was thinking about him too.
He doesn't say anything else. He doesn't need to. This is why you married him — not because he always knows what to say, but because he always knows when not to say anything at all.

choices.text: Thank you for being here.
Stay close today. I'm going to need you.

narrative.text: The car takes you to the Chancellor's residence. Vyktor has already arranged the first briefing folders on your desk. The ink on the oath is barely dry and the work has already begun.
Welcome to the job, Chancellor.

transition_to_work.monologue: The speech is done. The crowd has gone home. Tomorrow morning I sit in the cabinet room for the first time — nine chairs, nine names, nine problems waiting to become crises. Vyktor says six weeks before the goodwill runs out. I intend to make those six weeks count.

choices.text: Let's begin.
